extracted.intended_audience: trademark applicants and practitioners (attorneys/agents) engaged in concurrent use proceedings before the TTAB/USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules for preparing, instituting, defending, and proving entitlement in concurrent use trademark registration proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on amending to seek concurrent use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Trademark Act § 1051(a) an applicant may not amend the application to seek concurrent use until use is effected; applicants may not file an amendment to allege use in an application under § 1(b) that is the subject of an opposition; 37 C.F.R. § 2.76(a) prohibits filing an amendment to allege use after the application has been approved for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot convert an intent-to-use filing to seek concurrent registration until actual use occurs. See TMEP § 1207.04(b) and 37 C.F.R. § 2.99(g) for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackout period while opposition pending
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are in a 'blackout period' while an opposition is pending, during which certain amendments or actions (e.g., filing to allege use) are restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TMEP § 1104.03(b); an amendment to allege use may be impermissible during this period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon-and-refile option to pursue concurrent use
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant involved in an opposition may consider abandoning its opposed application and refiling it as a use-based concurrent use application; if abandonment is with opposer’s consent, judgment will not be entered and the opposition can be dismissed without prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment with consent avoids adverse judgment; opposer may also amend its own application to seek concurrent registration for full adjudication. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.135 and TBMP § 1113.01 for termination mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations when opposing registrant has incontestable registration
rubrics_metrics.description: An incontestable registration (Trademark Act § 15) is subject to a concurrent use proceeding, but any registration issued to the concurrent use applicant as against the owner of an incontestable registration will be limited to applicant’s area of actual use prior to actual or constructive notice of registrant’s rights, unless parties stipulate otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even prior users may receive geographically limited registrations when facing incontestable registrations. Case law: Boi Na Braza, Holiday Inn, Thriftimart (TTAB/CCPA examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolling of five-year incontestability period by concurrent use filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The five-year incontestability period for a registration is tolled with respect to an applicant’s concurrent rights if, before the five-year period expires, the applicant files a proper concurrent use application (or amends to seek concurrent use) naming the registrant as an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Arman’s Systems, Inc. v. Armand’s Subway, Inc., 215 USPQ 1048; follow timing requirements carefully to preserve concurrent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required marking/statement on applications approved for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application seeking concurrent registration is approved for publication, it is marked with a statement such as: 'SUBJECT TO CONCURRENT USE PROCEEDING WITH _____________. APPLICANT CLAIMS EXCLUSIVE RIGHT TO USE THE MARK IN THE AREA COMPRISING ______.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blanks are filled with involved application/registration numbers or names/addresses of parties and the area for which applicant seeks registration. Alternate templates apply when concurrent registration is based on prior Board determination or court decree (include proceeding/decree identifiers and prior involved application numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and status reporting for concurrent use applications
rubrics_metrics.description: After marking, the application is published in the Official Gazette with the indicated statement; the status changes to 'Concurrent Use Proceeding Pending' on the date of publication and the application is added to the Board’s electronic system and tracked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the application is unopposed (or oppositions dismissed/withdrawn) and meets specified conditions, it may go to issue without institution of a concurrent use proceeding (see 37 C.F.R. § 2.99(f), TBMP §§ 1103.02-.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances requiring institution of a concurrent use proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrent use proceeding will be instituted if: (1) the application seeks concurrent registration by way of a Board proceeding and is not opposed (or oppositions dismissed/withdrawn); (2) the application seeks concurrent registration based on a court decree but does not meet 37 C.F.R. § 2.99(f); or (3) the application seeks concurrent registration based on a prior Board determination but does not meet TBMP § 1103.02 conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the opposition period expires with no unresolved oppositions, the Board institutes the proceeding, identifies defending users, and sends notice to each party. There is no fee for institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and inclusion of involved applications/registrations in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board identifies and enters into the record any applications or registrations to be included in the concurrent use proceeding; if an involved application has not been published or cleared its opposition period, its owner is included as a common law user rather than as an applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may suspend proceedings at its discretion until an unpublished application becomes abandoned or survives the opposition period, after which the owner's status changes to applicant. See TBMP §§ 1104 and 1108.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice content, distribution, and service for commencement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no complaint; instead the Board prepares and sends notices to each concurrent use applicant and each excepted/defending party advising of institution, providing a web link to Office records, setting the due date for filing an 'answer', and specifying conferencing, disclosure, discovery, trial and briefing periods (subject to exceptions). Notices must include extensive identifying information for each involved party (names, addresses, attorneys/representatives, mark, goods/services, filing/registration dates and numbers, and claimed territory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices are sent to applicants (care of attorney/representative if any), involved users and registrants, or to domestic representatives where appointed. Email may be used if provided; undelivered Board notices may be remedied by publication in the Official Gazette. The Board no longer forwards copies of each concurrent use application with the notice and applicants need not provide copies for service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial schedule issuance variations
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution order will set conferencing, disclosures, discovery, trial and briefing periods unless there is more than one named excepted user and none owns a trademark application or registration; in that case, the trial schedule is issued after all answers are filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the proceeding is commenced solely to order a registrant to show cause for restricting its registration, the Board does not include a trial schedule with the notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locating excepted users: applicant's obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The concurrent use applicant bears the burden of providing current addresses of each specified excepted user and information concerning each user's use of its mark in its area/mode of use and any registrations/applications owned by the excepted user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a Board notice is returned undeliverable, the applicant must investigate and furnish the correct address. If the excepted user does not own an application/registration and the correct address cannot be furnished, the proceeding cannot go forward unless the applicant moves to amend its application to delete the user and provides factual basis for that motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when registrant excepted user cannot be located (petition to cancel)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant cannot locate the owner of a registration named as an excepted user, the applicant may file a petition to cancel the registration on grounds of abandonment; the concurrent use proceeding is suspended until the petition outcome; if cancellation is granted, applicant may move to amend to delete the registrant and seek an unrestricted registration; notice of the petition is published and default judgment may be entered if registrant fails to appear within the prescribed period (typically 30 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful cancellation for abandonment allows resumption of the concurrent use proceeding and possible amendment to seek geographically unrestricted registration if no other excepted users remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer requirement, timing, and default consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no complaint; the Board's notice informs parties of the due date for an 'answer' (usually 40 days). Applicants/registrants whose application/registration is involved are not required to answer but may do so; other specified parties (e.g., common law users) must file answers or risk default. Failure to file an answer when required results in judgment entered against that party precluding it from claiming any right more extensive than that acknowledged by applicant in the concurrent use application(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where default judgment is entered against a party, the concurrent use applicant still bears the burden of proving entitlement to registration as against that party. Defaulting parties will not continue to receive all Board communications, but will be mailed a copy of the Board’s final decision and must be served with any proposed amendment narrowing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and party seniority/juniority rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant for concurrent registration has the burden of proving entitlement to registration as against every party specified in its application; party seniority/juniority is determined by filing dates (latest filing date = junior party). Per 37 C.F.R. § 2.116(b), a junior party stands in the position of plaintiff against every senior party, and a senior party is a defendant against every junior party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applications share the same filing date, the application with the latest date of execution is deemed latest. A person specified as an excepted user who has not filed an application is considered senior to every party that has an application involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core issues to be proven in the proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal issue is the entitlement of the concurrent use applicant(s) to the registration(s) sought, and the extent, if any, to which every other involved application or registration should be restricted as a result; the Board does not determine the territorial rights of common law users unless they file an application and a concurrent use proceeding is instituted for that application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entitlement includes proving there will be no likelihood of confusion and proving concurrent lawful use in commerce prior to the applicable date specified in Trademark Act § 2(d) (usually use prior to earliest involved filing date or 1946 Act registrations, etc.). See TBMP § 1103.01(b),(d)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific matters/defenses other parties may assert
rubrics_metrics.description: Any other party may attempt to prove any ground or basis for refusal of registration that could be asserted against an unrestricted registration (e.g., bad faith junior user, failure to meet jurisdictional prior use date, unlawful use), or that applicant is entitled only to registration covering some of the area specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board decisions and cases illustrate common grounds: overlapping advertising, expansion beyond claimed territories, insufficient proof of territorial limits; consent alone may be insufficient to show entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte showing as proof route when only defaulting common-law users remain
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proceeding involves only the concurrent use applicant and one or more specified common law excepted users who have defaulted, the applicant may prove entitlement by making an ex parte showing (declarations/affidavits) rather than through formal trial procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte submissions should address many of the factors the Board considers at settlement agreements; if the ex parte showing is insufficient, judgment will be entered against the applicant and the registration refused. See TBMP § 1110 for settlement-factor guidance.
